books.section: Topic 8.13 The environment and natural resources from 1968 to 1980

primary_sources: EPA, 'The Birth of EPA' and EPA History 1970-1985 (dates)

source: original; stimulus is a table of federal environmental actions

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from EPA histories: NEPA signed January 1, 1970; EPA opened December 2, 1970; Clean Air Act signed December 1970; Clean Water Act enacted October 18, 1972; Endangered Species Act enacted December 28, 1973; DDT uses cancelled in 1972. Dates verified against EPA, 'The Birth of EPA,' EPA History 1970-1985, and the Duke Nicholas School environmental timeline. Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.13; 5 Steps Ch. 28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text:
Major federal environmental actions, 1970-1973:

| Action | Date | What it did |
| National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) | January 1, 1970 | Required federal agencies to assess the environmental effects of their projects |
| Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) | December 2, 1970 | New federal agency to enforce environmental laws |
| Clean Air Act | 1970 | Set national standards for air quality and auto emissions |
| Clean Water Act | October 18, 1972 | Set federal limits on pollutants discharged into waters |
| Endangered Species Act | December 28, 1973 | Protected species at risk of extinction and their habitats |
| DDT ban | December 31, 1972 | EPA ended nearly all uses of the pesticide DDT |

stem: Which statement best explains why the Endangered Species Act was a major expansion of federal power?

options.text: It gave the states full control over wildlife.
options.misconception: The table says the act protected species and habitats, a federal job, not a gift of control to the states.

options.text: It ended all hunting and fishing in the United States.
options.misconception: Background: The act protected listed species; it did not end all hunting and fishing.

options.text: It applied only to animals in zoos.
options.misconception: The table says the act protected species and their habitats, not only zoo animals.

options.text: It let Washington protect a species even when that limited building.

rationales.A: The table says the act protected species and habitats, a federal job, not a gift of control to the states.
rationales.B: Background: The act protected listed species; it did not end all hunting and fishing.
rationales.C: The table says the act protected species and their habitats, not only zoo animals.
rationales.D: Background: Protecting a species and its habitat meant Washington could block dams, roads, and other projects, which put federal power ahead of local development.
rationales.general:
1. The table says the act protected species at risk of extinction and their habitats.
2. Background: Habitat is land, so protecting it meant the federal government could limit what was built on that land.
3. Background: That power to stop a project for a single species was new, and it is why the act was a major expansion of federal power.
Remember: Follow the power: ask who can now say no, and to what.
